(1) the use of the term'supervenience' in philosophy has not been sufficiently precise to permit the use of a single definition, and (2) the term is best used in a way that is consistent with its original use in mathematics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the possibility of causation by supervenient properties.
the question of how the causal powers of a higher-level property depend on the causal powers of its lower-level base properties.
the causal efficacy of properties and their supervenient properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a supervening property, in virtue of its being a supervenient property, is not a cause, but that it may have causal relevance, and may even figure in a causal explanation of an effect.
the supervenience base of a supervenient property is causally relevant to the effects of the latter.
a supervenient property is causally efficacious in the sense that it can cause or contribute to the production of an effect, provided that the effect is not a supervenient effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mental events are caused by physical events, and that mental events cause physical events.
the mental supervenes on the physical and the mental causes physical events, but the mental is not efficacious in causing physical events.
supervenient causality, in a way, is a kind of 'program explanation'.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the case of mental properties, the causal efficacy of the supervenience base can be fully captured by the supervening mental properties, which can then be used to explain the behavior of the system in question, without any further causal contribution of the base (Kim 2005: 27).
supervenient properties can play a genuine causal role in the world, even if they do not have causal efficacy in themselves.
supervenience is a causal concept.
